items.title: Adding methotrexate to boost a refractory-gout drug
items.summary: In the MIRROR randomized trial, people with hard-to-control gout who took methotrexate alongside the infused medicine pegloticase reached the treatment goal far more often than those given pegloticase alone (about 71% versus 39% at six months). Combining the two also lowered the rate of infusion reactions. The trial focused on severe, treatment-resistant gout.
items.whyItMatters: For severe gout that has not responded to usual treatment, this trial supports a combination approach some specialists now use.

items.title: Long-term look at febuxostat and heart safety
items.summary: The FAST trial followed more than 6,000 people with gout taking either febuxostat or allopurinol and found febuxostat was not linked to a higher rate of serious heart-related events over long-term follow-up. The result offered reassurance alongside earlier, more mixed findings. It was an open-label trial in patients already being treated for gout.
items.whyItMatters: If a doctor prescribes febuxostat, this trial is part of the safety evidence behind that choice.

items.title: Updated US guideline centers on treat-to-target
items.summary: The American College of Rheumatology's 2020 gout guideline placed a treat-to-target strategy at the center of care, recommending that urate-lowering therapy be adjusted to reach and hold a serum urate goal. It named allopurinol as the preferred first medicine and emphasized anti-inflammatory flare prophylaxis when treatment begins. The guideline was built on a systematic review of the evidence.
items.whyItMatters: This guideline shapes how many clinicians in the US plan long-term gout treatment today.

items.title: Nurse-led care helped more patients hit target
items.summary: A randomized trial in the UK compared nurse-led gout care that included patient education and treat-to-target dosing against usual general-practice care. After two years, the large majority of the nurse-led group had reached the serum urate target, compared with a minority in usual care. The nurse-led group also tended to have fewer flares.
items.whyItMatters: It shows how education and steady follow-up, not just the medicine itself, can improve gout control.

items.title: Earlier trial raised a heart-safety question
items.summary: The CARES trial studied people with gout who also had heart disease and reported more heart-related and overall deaths among those taking febuxostat than those taking allopurinol, even though the two were similar on the main combined heart outcome. The finding prompted closer scrutiny of febuxostat. Later studies such as FAST added a fuller picture.
items.whyItMatters: It explains why a history of heart disease can influence which urate-lowering medicine a doctor chooses.
items.sourceName: New England Journal of Medicine (CARES trial)

items.title: European recommendations on managing gout
items.summary: The 2016 update of the European recommendations reaffirmed treating to a serum urate target and put patient education at the heart of gout care. They advised discussing urate-lowering therapy from diagnosis and using flare prophylaxis during the first months of treatment. The update drew on a systematic review of the evidence.
items.whyItMatters: These recommendations guide how many clinicians in Europe plan ongoing gout treatment.

items.title: Lower-dose colchicine for a flare
items.summary: The AGREE trial tested colchicine for an early gout flare and found a lower-dose schedule worked about as well as a higher-dose one while causing far fewer digestive side effects. The results supported using less colchicine to treat flares. Guidelines have since reflected the lower-dose approach.
items.whyItMatters: This is the evidence behind the smaller colchicine doses many doctors now use for flares.
